title: Build Custom Validation Framework Using Spring AOP
question: Your company has 50+ microservices, each with their own validation logic scattered across controllers and services. Management wants to centralize validation to ensure consistency. You need to build a custom validation framework using Spring AOP that: 1) Validates method parameters based on custom annotations (@ValidEmail, @ValidPhone, @ValidCreditCard), 2) Supports field-level and cross-field validation, 3) Returns standardized validation error responses, 4) Logs all validation failures to a central logging system, 5) Allows per-service customization. Design the aspect, pointcut expressions, advice type, custom annotations, and exception handling strategy. Discuss performance implications of validation in aspects.
realWorldScenario: Building centralized validation framework with AOP

title: Design Audit Logging System Using Spring AOP
question: Build an audit logging system for a financial application that tracks all service method calls, capturing: who called the method, when, with what parameters, the return value, execution time, and whether it succeeded or failed. Requirements: 1) Audit specific service methods annotated with @Audited, 2) Mask sensitive data (passwords, SSN, credit cards) in logs, 3) Write audit logs asynchronously to avoid performance impact, 4) Store in database for compliance (7-year retention), 5) Support different audit levels (BASIC, DETAILED, FULL). Design the aspect, advice type, asynchronous processing strategy, sensitive data masking approach, and how to handle high-volume logging without impacting application performance.
realWorldScenario: Building production audit logging with AOP and async processing

title: Implement Multi-Tenancy Using Spring DI and Scopes
question: Design a multi-tenant SaaS application where each tenant has isolated database, cache, and configuration. The application serves 1000+ tenants. A single application instance handles requests for all tenants. You need to: 1) Identify the tenant from request header/subdomain, 2) Route database connections to the correct tenant database, 3) Isolate cache per tenant, 4) Load tenant-specific configuration (features, themes, limits), 5) Ensure no data leakage between tenants. Use Spring's DI, bean scopes, and custom scopes to design the solution. Discuss: tenant identification strategy, DataSource routing, custom bean scope for tenant context, thread safety, and performance considerations for 1000+ tenants.
realWorldScenario: Building multi-tenant SaaS with tenant isolation

title: Design Feature Toggle System Using Spring Profiles and Conditional Beans
question: Your team uses feature toggles for gradual rollouts and A/B testing. You need a feature toggle system that: 1) Enables/disables features without deployment, 2) Supports user-based toggles (show feature to 10% of users), 3) Environment-based toggles (feature in staging, not prod), 4) Time-based toggles (enable on specific date), 5) Real-time toggle updates from a config server. Design using Spring @Profile, @Conditional, and custom conditions. Discuss: how to implement percentage-based rollouts, dynamic bean registration/deregistration, configuration refresh without restart, and caching strategy for toggle evaluations to avoid performance overhead.
realWorldScenario: Building feature toggle system with dynamic configuration

title: Build Resilient Retry Mechanism Using Spring AOP
question: Your microservices make calls to external APIs (payment gateway, shipping provider, notification service) that occasionally fail due to network issues or rate limiting. Build a retry framework using Spring AOP that: 1) Automatically retries failed method calls, 2) Supports configurable retry count and backoff strategies (linear, exponential), 3) Only retries on specific exceptions (network errors, not business exceptions), 4) Implements circuit breaker pattern (stop retrying if service is down), 5) Logs retry attempts and publishes metrics. Design the aspect, custom annotation @Retryable(maxAttempts, backoff, retryOn), backoff calculation, circuit breaker state management, and how to avoid retry storms.
realWorldScenario: Building resilient retry with circuit breaker

title: Design Application Warm-Up Using Bean Lifecycle Hooks
question: Your Spring Boot application takes 2 minutes to handle the first request after startup (cold start) due to lazy loading, cache warming, and connection pool initialization. This causes timeouts in health checks and poor user experience. Design a warm-up mechanism using bean lifecycle hooks that: 1) Warms up caches by pre-loading frequently accessed data, 2) Initializes connection pools and HTTP clients, 3) Runs smoke tests to verify external dependencies, 4) Delays marking the application as 'ready' until warm-up completes, 5) Provides progress visibility (logging/metrics). Use @PostConstruct, InitializingBean, ApplicationListener, and readiness probes. Discuss: parallel warm-up for speed, handling warm-up failures, and distinguishing liveness from readiness.
realWorldScenario: Optimizing application startup with warm-up strategy

title: Implement Dynamic DataSource Routing for Read-Write Splitting
question: Your application uses a primary database for writes and multiple read replicas for reads to scale read traffic. Design a dynamic DataSource routing solution using Spring that: 1) Routes write operations to primary, read operations to replicas, 2) Load-balances reads across replicas, 3) Automatically detects method intent (read vs write) using AOP or transaction annotations, 4) Handles replication lag (reads after writes should go to primary), 5) Removes failed replicas from rotation. Use Spring's AbstractRoutingDataSource, ThreadLocal for context, and @Transactional(readOnly). Discuss: determining read vs write operations, handling replication lag, replica health checks, and thread safety.
realWorldScenario: Database read-write splitting with dynamic routing

title: Design Event-Driven Saga Using Spring Application Events
question: Implement a distributed transaction across multiple services (OrderService, PaymentService, InventoryService, ShippingService) using the Saga pattern with Spring events. When an order is placed: 1) Reserve inventory, 2) Process payment, 3) Create shipment. Each step can fail, requiring compensating transactions. Design using Spring ApplicationEvent, @EventListener, and @TransactionalEventListener. Requirements: 1) Handle partial failures with compensation, 2) Ensure exactly-once event processing, 3) Maintain saga state (which steps completed), 4) Implement timeout for long-running sagas, 5) Provide saga visibility (status dashboard). Discuss: event ordering guarantees, idempotency, saga state persistence, failure recovery, and why you'd use events vs orchestration.

title: Build Plugin Architecture Using Spring DI and ClassLoader
question: Design a plugin system where third-party developers can extend your application by dropping JAR files into a plugins directory. Requirements: 1) Plugins discovered and loaded at runtime, 2) Each plugin has its own Spring context (isolation), 3) Plugins can provide implementations of core interfaces (e.g., AuthenticationProvider, NotificationProvider), 4) Plugins can be enabled/disabled without restart, 5) Plugin dependencies don't conflict with main application. Design using Spring's parent-child contexts, custom ClassLoaders, and @ComponentScan. Discuss: plugin discovery mechanism, class loading isolation, sharing beans between plugin and main context, plugin lifecycle management, and security concerns.

title: Implement Request Correlation ID Tracking Across Services
question: In a microservices architecture with 20+ services, tracking a request across services is challenging. Implement a correlation ID system using Spring that: 1) Generates correlation ID for incoming requests (if not present), 2) Propagates correlation ID to all outgoing HTTP calls, async tasks, and message queues, 3) Includes correlation ID in all logs (MDC), 4) Works with RestTemplate, WebClient, and async @Async methods, 5) No code changes needed in business logic. Use Spring interceptors, filters, ThreadLocal/MDC, and AOP. Discuss: ThreadLocal propagation to async tasks, handling reactive programming (WebFlux), cleaning up ThreadLocal to avoid memory leaks, and ensuring correlation ID survives thread pool handoffs.
realWorldScenario: Distributed request tracing with correlation IDs
